data.title: Gold bulls not capitulating... yet
data.description:
Key points:
  • Stoxx 600 down 1.5%, volatility at highest since April
  • European tech index down 4% on day, 9% on week
  • Tech set for biggest weekly fall since late 2020
  • Asia ex Japan shares post biggest weekly fall since 2020
  • US futures lower, VIX above 30

GOLD BULLS NOT CAPITULATING… YET

Gold extended its sharp selloff as higher real yields and a stronger dollar sap its appeal, with the key question now being whether the metal is poised for a recovery.

According to Joni Teves, strategist at UBS Investment Bank, a recovery may require patience.

“For now, there is little urgency to move away from those themes and into gold,” he says after mentioning Fed rate hikes and S&P returns driven by AI.

“More important, though, is what we are not seeing: widespread capitulation,” he adds.

“The resilience of gold ETF holdings supports that view, and we expect broader over-the-counter (OTC) investor holdings to show similar durability.”

And if something goes wrong, gold could come back into favour.

“Debt and fiscal concerns continue to underpin investors’ interest in gold,” UBS’ Teves argues.

“There is also a lingering worry that something could break—whether through disappointment in AI, an overshoot in bond yields or monetary policy missteps. Those risks could ultimately lead to weak or negative growth and substantially lower real yields.”

(Stefano Rebaudo)

The package brings together activities involving more than 150 countries plus the European Union, 37 cities and more than 260 businesses, from expanding electricity grids to electrifying transport and industry.

Among the results highlighted were more than 21,000 kilometers of electricity grids built in 2025 and annual investment plans of at least $156 billion for grids, renewable energy and storage.

But UN climate chief Simon Stiell acknowledged that the benefits must reach further.

'Vulnerable developing countries need affordable finance and technology. Workers and communities must help to shape and be supported through major change. Across the board, we need to move far faster to meet the demands of the science,' he said.

data.title: Apple seems to be building its own AI agent. This could be bad news for Meta's Muse.
data.description:
By Nora Redmond

Shares in Apple edged higher in Friday's premarket trading.

Apple appears to be working on its own autonomous artificial-intelligence agent following the success of Meta Platform's recently-launched Muse AI assistant.

The development became evident when the iPhone maker added a number of job listings to its website in the past few days seeking candidates that can help with the plans. In one opening for a senior engineering manager in Santa Clara, Ca., the technology giant said it is looking for someone who can lead a team building agentic AI agents.

The company said that the agents would have several capabilities, including understanding users' complex goals, deconstructing requests with multiple different questions, conducting thorough research and combining knowledge with users' personal contexts.

Another post recruiting a machine learning engineer in Tel Aviv, Israel, said the person would "design and build agentic systems featuring multi-agent coordination, long-horizon reasoning, tool use, and planning frameworks."

Shares in Apple (AAPL) advanced 0.5% in premarket trading on Friday, whereas Meta's stock (META) declined almost 2%.

It comes after the company behind Facebook saw its AI assistant Muse become a viral hit after its launch on Sept. 8, sitting at the top of Apple's App Store listings of free apps consecutively for almost two weeks. It's now the second-most popular app, behind only TikTok. At the time of its release, Meta said its agent was intended to answer questions as well as complete tasks for users.

JPMorgan raised its price target for the stock following the launch of Muse, referring to the system as "an extremely capable personal agent" with the potential of reaching billions of users worldwide.

"We continue to believe this is the first of many steps to bring tens and potentially hundreds of millions of businesses onto Muse, and form the foundation for monetization," Doug Anmuth, head of U.S. internet equity research, at the investment bank, said of the agent's e-commerce partnerships.

Meta reported higher-than-expected revenue in its third quarter, posting a year-on-year jump of 26% to $64.60 billion, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighting the rapid uptake of Muse.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley, led by Brian Nowak, said that Muse remains the early leader in agentic AI systems, calling its high adoption so far "encouraging for Muse's longer-term monetization potential."

But now, Apple seems to be racing to develop its own competing AI agent as hyperscalers race to dominate in the field.

Apple did not respond to MarketWatch's request for comment.

-Nora Redmond

data.title: Enel agrees US solar deal, taking North America renewables to 13.5 GW
data.description:

data.title: EU's Hansen says US trade uncertainty is drawing Mexico, Europe closer
data.description:
Key points:
  • Mexico could ratify interim deal by end-2026, commissioner says
  • Hansen says US uncertainty pushing partners to other models
  • US declined to extend North America trade pact in July
  • EU-Mexico pact would strip tariffs from bulk of food trade

By Sarah Morland

EU agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen expects Mexico to clear a final hurdle for a new EU trade pact to take effect by the end of the year, just as uncertainty over access to the US market brings Mexico and EU interests closer together.

The EU and Mexico in May signed a modernization of their 2000 trade agreement after close to a decade of long-stalled negotiations, but Mexico's Senate needs to ratify an interim version of the agreement before it can take effect.

The deal would, once in force, cut tariffs for the overwhelming bulk of bilateral food trade.

The US is the biggest trade partner for both Mexico and the EU, but on-and-off tariff threats under US President Donald Trump's second term in office have thrown long-established supply chains into uncertainty.

"The current geopolitical situation is bringing together those of us who want a different system, a different model for trade - one based on speaking as equals, not just the law of the strongest," Hansen said in an interview while on a trade visit to Mexico City.

The EU ratified the interim deal, a gateway to the broader EU-Mexico Modernised Global Agreement, in July.

That same month, the US declined to extend the North American free trade pact, kicking off a process of annual reviews that throw into question the terms of US-Mexican trade worth an annual $960 billion.

The US is by far Mexico's largest trade partner and buys roughly 80% of its exports. Mexico's dependence on the US market exposes its economy to Trump's repeated use of tariff threats to influence domestic policy.

Hansen suggested the ongoing US-Mexico trade talks could be slowing Mexico's ratification of the EU deal, but said talks with Mexican officials gave him a "good feeling" the Senate could vote through the European pact by the end of this year.

Mexico's Economy Ministry told Reuters the Senate was yet to schedule a date for the interim deal's ratification. This deal takes effect following a period after both sides inform each other their internal ratifications are complete.

Hansen added that Mexico and Europe's culture of good food makes them natural allies over the protection of denominations of origin - restricting labels like champagne and tequila to the regions where they are traditionally produced.

Washington has long opposed such denominations and argues they limit free trade, but the EU-Mexico deal would dramatically expand such protections in Mexico, home to over 130 million people and the US' biggest export market.

Mexican products such as avocado, chili, cocoa and tequila should see good growth prospects in the EU, Hansen said, while the EU hopes to increase exports of pork, chicken and dairy.

While tariffs have hurt Mexican producers and pushed up US food costs, Hansen said they are also opening new possibilities.

"If it's harder to access the US market, then it's only natural we look elsewhere," he said.

data.title: Congress struggles to avert US shutdown as Iran war divides lawmakers
data.description:
Key points:
  • Current federal funding expires after December 11, leaving Congress three weeks to reach a deal
  • Senate bipartisan funding package would need 60 votes to pass in 100-seat chamber
  • Democrats split on tying agency funding to limits on Trump's military action against Iran

By David Morgan

Congress could be headed for a pre-Christmas government shutdown as divisions over the Iran war and President Donald Trump's demand for $350 billion in new Pentagon spending threaten to derail any funding deal, lawmakers from both parties warn.

Lawmakers have only three weeks to iron out an agreement to keep federal agencies operating after December 11, when current funding is set to expire. But the two parties remained far apart as they prepared for a one-week Thanksgiving holiday break, especially in the 100-seat Senate, where a bipartisan funding package would need 60 votes to pass.

Republicans and Democrats aim to find common ground on a stopgap measure to fund government operations into early next year, when Democrats take control of the Senate and House of Representatives after a sweeping victory in the November midterms. They also hold out hope of passing some full-year appropriations bills in the current lame-duck session to fund parts of the government through the current fiscal year, which ends on September 30.

But each party faces its own dilemma over how to move forward. Republicans are hesitant to pursue the partisan path Trump has demanded on defense funding, citing differences over what should be included in such a bill. Democrats are divided over whether limiting funding for the president's Iran war is worth a government shutdown.

'WE DON'T WANT TO FUND THE WAR'

Republicans have sought to paint Democrats as willing to trigger the fourth partial government shutdown of Trump's second term, claiming that Democrats have not been willing to negotiate a funding package before a December 1 party leadership election between current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and challenger Chris Van Hollen.

"The American people don't need another government shutdown," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week. "I think that would be a colossal mistake and a real disservice to the people of this country."

But Senate Democrats acknowledged that they are wrestling with the question of whether to insist on language to restrict Trump's use of force against Iran, a prospect that most Republicans reject, even if it means cutting off funds to federal agencies and workers ahead of the Christmas holiday.

"The big obstacle is that we don't want to fund the war, we don't want to shut down, how do you solve that," said Senator Peter Welch, a Vermont Democrat. "That's the Gordian knot."

Democrats have already forced three shutdowns since Trump returned to power in January 2025, including the longest large-scale shutdown in US history. Earlier this year, they cut off Homeland Security funding after federal immigration agents fatally shot two US citizens in Minneapolis.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, declined to state his own position on funding but suggested that the pain American families are now suffering from high energy prices due to the Iran war could justify another cutoff of funding.

"A shutdown of government right before the holidays is a tough nut. You wouldn't do it if it wasn't dire. This is pretty dire. The war's gone on for a long time, and I think we saw in the election that it's very unpopular," Hickenlooper told reporters.

Some Democrats adamantly oppose a shutdown.

"Shutting the government down doesn't stop the war," said Representative Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. "Everybody feels very strongly. They want to end this war ... How do you strategically move to get that done? Without shutting down the government - that's where I am on this issue."

'WE'RE GOING TO RUN OUT OF TIME'

Senate Republicans have failed to agree on whether to meet Trump's $350 billion defense funding request through a partisan maneuver called budget reconciliation, which would allow them to circumvent Democratic opposition and enact such legislation with a simple majority vote.

The Senate Republican conference discussed the issue behind closed doors for more than an hour this week and decided instead to pursue bipartisan talks with Democrats on a $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill proposed by Republicans that contains only $69 billion of Trump's funding request.

Republicans say reconciliation remains on the table, which could complicate a bipartisan deal.

"We're going to run out of time if we don't expedite either more communications with both sides of the aisle, or if we can't come to a consensus on exactly what it is would be in a reconciliation product," Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Reuters.

Republicans and Democrats both held out the possibility of passing at least some of the 12 full-year appropriations bills needed to fully fund federal agencies for the remainder of fiscal 2027 and funding the remainder of government agencies through a stopgap known as a continuing resolution or CR.

"Being able to finish all 12 bills is not possible. But I believe we can get out a number of them ... and then deal with where we need to be on the CR," DeLauro said.

data.title: Brazilian students turn to burned fish bones as clean water filter
data.description:
By Bruno Kelly

A group of Brazilian high school students and their teacher have come up with a local solution for providing clean drinking water in remote areas of the Amazon: a filter made of charcoal produced by burning the bones of the region's giant pirarucu fish.

The process involves heating the chunky vertebrae of the fish — which typically grow to 2 meters (6.6 feet) in length — to as much as 900 degrees Celsius (1,650 degrees Fahrenheit) and then grinding the charred bones into a powder that absorbs heavy metals and other pollutants.

"It's a sustainable, ecological form of carbon that does not require the felling of trees," said Galileu da Silva Pires, a biology teacher at the Jose Mota school in Manacapuru, a town on the Solimoes River, about 100 km (62 miles) west of Manaus. "It means we can produce drinking water with this new resource."

Communities living on the banks of rivers in the Amazon region often are exposed to hazardous drinking water during droughts when rainwater becomes unavailable and lower water levels in rivers cause concentrated levels of pollutants.

Water levels in the Solimoes River, the upper stretch of the Amazon River, are currently low after a period of drought.

Da Silva Pires said work by his students on the project could be used in communities elsewhere, too.

"This shows the potential these kids have," he said. "You take a problem that has been around for decades, and with natural resources you can find solutions."

Charred fish bones have previously been recognized as a way to filter water without resorting to felling trees for timber. But the use of pirarucu bones also could help to reduce another environmental problem in the Amazon region — the accumulation of fish waste after the meat is eaten by people.

"We feel great about getting better quality water, filtered water, creating something of value," said student Ana Flavia Costa Lopes, 18.

data.title: Big Pharma, with eye on Anthropic, says AI is shrinking drug discovery timelines
data.description:
Key points:
  • AI already yielding concrete results in preclinical development
  • AI companies want to cure disease and are in the market for data to build out models
  • Big pharma views AI companies as potential partners and competitors

By Michael Erman, Bhanvi Satija and Patrick Wingrove

Artificial intelligence has sped up early-stage drug development work at some of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies this year, cutting by as much as half the time it takes to produce new molecules and move them into the clinic, according to their top scientists.

GSK , Bristol Myers Squibb , Novartis , Eli Lilly , Novo Nordisk , AstraZeneca and Sanofi all say they have moved beyond less glamorous tasks for AI like preparing regulatory filings. They are now using the technology for designing molecules, sorting out the most promising ones, and identifying safety risks.

“There is no part of the discovery through development pipeline where we are not using AI,” AstraZeneca executive Sharon Barr said.

Some of the scientists say decades of drug discovery experience and data give them an advantage over AI companies like Anthropic , which is gearing up to be a rival, partner or both, with a $1.5 trillion initial public offering this week.

In recent months, it opened its own laboratory and announced other investments, part of pushing AI to speed drug discovery.

On Thursday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, at the Nasdaq before shares began trading, spoke of his father dying of a disease shortly before a cure was found.

Although clinical trials and experiments will still take time, he said, "I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future, fewer families miss a cure by a few years."

Drug companies are gauging whether the upstart can succeed in tackling disease. Historically, nearly 9 out of 10 drugs developed using conventional methods fail in clinical trials. It can cost billions of dollars and take 10 to 15 years to bring a drug to market, according to industry lobby group PhRMA.

Aliza Apple, who runs Lilly's TuneLab, which gives smaller biotechs access to some of the drugmaker's internal AI models to promote collaboration, said claims like those made by Amodei and the founders of Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs that the technology is capable of curing all disease overstate current capabilities.

“It would be great for them to cure one, and then let's talk about the rest,” she said.

CONCRETE RESULTS

Pharma company scientists say their AI programs are already yielding concrete results.

Sanofi said it saved at least a year developing asthma treatment lunsekimig using an AI-enabled approach to translate early biology into clinical decisions that let the company skip a dose-selection study. Novartis said AI tools helped it find five targets it prioritized for developing kidney disease treatments.

Bristol Myers said one of its sickle cell anemia candidates would not have been developed without the company's AI systems. It's using AI to refine new molecules and run simulations based on its trial data to determine which ones should progress, Chief Research Officer Robert Plenge said.

"The next area for us is to tie those models into laboratory automation... to make better, high-quality molecules faster,” he added.

Novo Nordisk said AI has cut the number of cycles of designing, manufacturing and testing new molecules from around eight to three and slashed the time of each cycle from eight weeks to four.

Still, the number of AI-enabled drugs in clinical testing has only climbed incrementally. In March, researchers identified 129 drug candidates across 69 companies, up from around 117 eight months earlier. Most of the programs remain in early-stage development.

“I think over the next 1, 2, 3 years we'll see a sharp uptick in AI drugs being developed pre-clinically and also drugs that go to clinical trials,” said Dr. Waqas Haque, an oncology fellow at University of Chicago who was on the team that compiled the data.

“I don't know if those drugs are going to be more successful than non-AI drugs, and I don't think they're going to be approved any quicker,” he said, because of bottlenecks with human trials and regulators.

'JUST THE BEGINNING'

Anthropic's Amodei has long said curing disease is one of the main benefits AI can provide to humanity.

The company is working on its own and with partners like Bristol Myers to develop new drugs. It launched scientific research-focused AI software called Claude Science, and added Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan to its board. Other companies, including Novo Nordisk, use Anthropic models and Claude Science in their R&D work.

Luca Giani, senior principal at venture capital firm Alumni Ventures, said Anthropic — and rival frontier labs — are shopping for pharma-related acquisitions.

"They are out to get more data, and they are out to get more of the companies," Giani said.

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment on its acquisition plans and the nature of its relationship with drugmakers.

Even before its $1.5 trillion IPO, Anthropic announced several partnerships and an acquisition last month, he said.

"I think it's just the beginning."

Lilly’s Apple said Anthropic and AI rivals can be viewed as allies and competitors.

“In the early days, we certainly saw them as vendors. To be fair, that's how they framed themselves. I think we increasingly see them as collaborators,” Apple said. “A year ago they weren't doing any programs, and a year from now, it's anyone's guess.”

GSK Chief Scientific Officer Tony Wood said he views Anthropic “as another competitor,” while Bristol Myers and Novo see the AI companies more as partners.

Still, Novo said it does not provide proprietary data to frontier labs to train their AI models, nor does Sanofi.

“If you don’t have the data to train the model on, then it breaks down very quickly,” said Matt Truppo, global head of computational & AI strategy for Sanofi R&D.

Truppo said he expects AI to cut early-discovery timelines by 20% to 25% within two years, and perhaps by half within five years, across more than 100 drug development programs.

It may be some time before this can be expanded beyond treatment areas where the company has the most proprietary data, he added.

Novartis President of Biomedical Research Fiona Marshall said the average time from project start to a drug candidate has gone from three years to about 18 months to two years.

“We have had a lot of data," Marshall said, "and now we can really use that data in a much more sophisticated way.”

data.title: Astronomers observe a huge puffy star merge with smaller companion
data.description:
Key points:
  • Stars located in Milky Way's neighboring Andromeda Galaxy
  • Larger star was seven times more massive than the sun
  • It expanded in its death throes, engulfing its companion

By Will Dunham

Astronomers have observed a large dying star, seven times more massive and 18,000 times brighter than the sun, engulfing a smaller companion in a stellar merger unlike any other previously witnessed.

The merger involved a pair of stars that were bound gravitationally — known as a binary system — in which the larger one greatly expanded in its death throes into what is called a puffy supergiant and enveloped the smaller one, with the two stars then combining into one.

This cosmic connection occurred about 2.5 million light-years from Earth on the outskirts of the Andromeda Galaxy, one of our Milky Way's closest galactic neighbors. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km).

The researchers identified the impending engulfment nearly three years before it occurred and then watched as the merger unfolded, step by step.

"Giant stars engulfing their companion stars have been theorized for many decades, and understanding the outcomes of this process has important implications for explaining a wide range of systems that we see today in the universe," said Viraj Karambelkar, a postdoctoral researcher and NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York, lead author of the research published in the journal Nature.

"The system presented in this study provides the first direct observations of this process happening — the first time a giant star engulfing its companion was caught in the act," Karambelkar said.

Large stars near the end of their lifespan can swell up as their cores run out of fuel and shrink while the inner stellar heat pushes the outer layers outward. The larger star in this study puffed up to 350 times the sun's diameter. The smaller star, whose diameter was about 70% that of the sun, orbited its companion at roughly the same distance as between Mars and the sun, and was engulfed in the bigger star's expansion.

'SET OFF A BOMB'

The researchers detected brightening when this occurred in 2018, and the smaller star began to spiral inward toward the core of the bigger star over the next seven years. Toward the end of 2025, the smaller star finally merged with the core of the larger one, triggering an eruption a million times brighter than the sun in what Karambelkar called "a unification event."

"This violent collision set off a bomb inside the star, producing the bright eruption that we saw," Karambelkar said.

The researchers first spotted the stars using data from the infrared WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California and NASA's NEOWISE space telescope, then watched the events with the orbiting SPHEREx and James Webb space telescopes and various ground-based observatories.

"We have observed mergers of stars in the past," said Columbia astrophysics professor and study co-author Kishalay De.

"The difference is in the nature of the stars that merged. In the past, stellar mergers were observed from two stars that were fairly small and compact, and their merger was almost inevitable once they came into physical contact. However, the bigger star in this event was a very puffed-up star where its outer envelope was loosely bound. This configuration is exactly the kind in which a merger may or may not happen," De said.

In some cases, an engulfed smaller star might release enough energy to blow away the larger star's puffy outer layers, leaving behind the remaining core of the original bigger star orbiting the smaller one, De said.

While the larger of the two stars in this instance was nearing the end of its life, the merger may have produced a rejuvenated star with a new lease on life, the researchers said.

The researchers gave the merged star the nickname Bao, the name of popular steamed buns in Chinese cuisine.

"The auto-assigned name to this eruption was AT2025abao — 'Astronomical Transient in 2025 abao.' We called it Bao as an affectionate term derived from this. The similarity with the Chinese buns definitely encouraged us to adopt the nickname," Karambelkar said.

data.title: Anthropic listing extends Nasdaq's dominant run against arch-rival NYSE
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq IPOs raise about $201.8 billion this year versus $20.8 billion on NYSE, Dealogic data shows
  • Nasdaq finished ahead of NYSE six times in 2018 to 2025 period, according to Dealogic
  • New rules fast-track names like SpaceX into Nasdaq 100 index

By Anirban Sen

The market share battle between the two top US exchanges has never been so lopsided.

With Anthropic's record-breaking initial public offering on Wednesday, Nasdaq snatched another marquee listing from the New York Stock Exchange this year, adding to its already wide lead in the battle for market share against its downtown rival. The exchange displayed the Anthropic win on the huge screens that envelop its Times Square address on Thursday, as more than 800 million shares changed hands in the AI company's debut.

"Anthropic’s IPO is a very proud moment for us," said Adena Friedman, chief executive officer of Nasdaq, in an interview Thursday. "We’ve been engaging with the Anthropic team for a very long time. Separate from the entire listing experience, we've been a client to them, as we are to the AI ecosystem, and so we also have gotten to know them in that context as well."

Over the last decade, the listing advantage has swung decisively in Nasdaq's favor. According to data from Dealogic, there have been 64 IPOs — led by Anthropic and SpaceX — on Nasdaq so far this year, raising about $201.8 billion, dwarfing the $20.8 billion haul raised from 42 IPOs on NYSE.

That is the widest gap in terms of capital raised between the two exchanges record since Dealogic started tracking the data in 1995. In 2017, NYSE raked in share sale proceeds of $28.8 billion from 69 deals, versus Nasdaq's $9.3 billion haul from 86 flotations. However, Nasdaq finished ahead of NYSE six out of eight times between 2018 and 2025, according to Dealogic, and is on track to do so again this year.

Nasdaq’s run of dominance can be linked to several moves the exchange operator has made over the years. Friedman, who has led Nasdaq for a decade, on Thursday cited the exchange operator's strength in marketing IPOs, its investor relations business that helps connect companies with large asset managers and institutional investors, and its index business — which it launched in 1985 — as key competitive advantages.

These efforts have allowed it to build relationships with founders in big IPO hubs like Silicon Valley and contributed to its dominance in tech listings.

"It's a very hard problem (for NYSE) to solve because Nasdaq didn't build its private markets business or its index just two years ago. They have had a head start of several years compared to their competitors. NYSE will have to probably just copy what Nasdaq has done for the past 10 years," said Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street.

NYSE executives are under increasing pressure to win the next mega-IPO after the recent losses to Nasdaq, according to two people familiar with the matter. The NYSE did not respond to a request for comment.

"Probably the major reason (for their dominance) is that Nasdaq has their own indexes," said Lau, referring to the Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq Composite , which are licensed for use by institutional asset managers. "That is a very big draw for many companies such as SpaceX and Anthropic."

The Nasdaq 100's constituents include several of the world's most valuable companies, such as Apple , Nvidia and Alphabet .

STRATEGIC ADVANTAGE

Admission to benchmarks like the Nasdaq 100 or S&P 500 gives companies increased access to deep-pocketed institutions with large index funds. This broadens the companies' shareholder base and improves share liquidity. The NYSE has a similar index that tracks its 100 largest US stocks that it launched last year, but it is less widely followed by investors.

Nasdaq introduced new rules earlier this year to speed the addition of newly listed megacap companies to the index, a move experts say gives them another advantage over the NYSE, even as it has drawn criticism from some quarters.

In an interview with Bloomberg in May, NYSE President Lynn Martin called the rule changes "questionable." On Thursday, Friedman said only a handful of megacap companies of the size and scale of Anthropic and SpaceX have the potential to be fast-tracked into the Nasdaq 100, adding that market liquidity is not an issue.

Reuters reported in March that SpaceX made early inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 a necessary condition to list on the Nasdaq. The exchange ultimately added the company to the index 15 days after its stock market debut.

data.title: After 7 years in court, Meta says 9 million claims belong in arbitration
data.description:
By Jenna Greene

When Facebook and Instagram advertisers sued Meta in 2018, arguing that the company misrepresented the reach of their ads, the proposed class action initially proceeded much like any other high-stakes lawsuit.

There were motions, depositions and discovery—hundreds of docket entries over seven years until the case was finally set to go before a jury in San Francisco federal court.

That is, until the eve of trial last year, when Meta unveiled an unexpected argument. It said roughly 80% of the certified class, or about 9 million advertisers, were actually obliged to pursue their claims individually via private arbitration.

Plaintiffs' lawyers cried foul, arguing that arbitration isn’t something a defendant can hold in reserve for years while testing its fortunes in federal court.

The fight is now before the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals, where a three-judge panel this week wrestled with whether Meta forfeited its right to arbitrate by litigating in court for years.

Or as Judge Ryan Nelson put it, “There is a sandbagging problem here. We finally get to trial and you’re like, ‘Oh, I’ve got my get-out-of-jail-free card.’”

Meta argues that it never waived its right to arbitrate most advertisers’ claims, and that it gave notice of its intent to do so at the proper time – after the class was certified and members had been notified and given the chance to opt out.

A Meta spokesperson in an email said, “We stand by our arguments made in our briefs and before the court of appeals.”

The dispute arises amid a wider shift in the mass-arbitration landscape. Not long ago, the prospect of arbitrating 9 million individual claims would have spooked most companies. The filing fees alone — thousands of dollars per case, payable upfront — could create enormous pressure on defendants to settle, regardless of the merits.

But major arbitration providers, including the American Arbitration Association and JAMS, have spent the last several years rewriting their mass-arbitration procedures, reducing the ability of plaintiffs to use those costs as leverage.

The changes appear to be altering some companies' calculations. Amazon, for example, reinstated its mandatory consumer arbitration provisions in August after doing away with the requirement five years ago.

Here, Meta’s arbitration agreement includes a provision barring claimants from litigating as a class, allowing the company to dodge the risk of being hit with a single, enormous judgment.

But there's a wrinkle. Advertisers that bought ads before the arbitration provision took effect in 2018 — roughly 20% of the class — are not bound by it. Both sides agree those claims dating back to 2014 will remain in federal court regardless of what the 9th Circuit decides.

“We always were going to have to litigate. This is a mixed class,” Meta lawyer Samir Deger-Sen, a partner at Latham & Watkins, told the 9th Circuit panel on Monday, rejecting the idea that Meta's federal court efforts were inconsistent with its arbitration rights.

He said the remaining class tops 2 million people “with hundreds of millions of dollars worth of recovery.”

The plaintiffs allege Meta charged artificially high premiums for ad placements by inflating the number of consumers that ads on its platform might reach. Meta in court papers denies the allegations.

Meta does concede that it relinquished its right to invoke arbitration against the two named plaintiffs, DZ Reserve, an e-commerce business, and Cain Maxwell, which sold weapons accessories.

Instead, the dispute turns on the unnamed class members --- millions of individuals and businesses that placed ads on Meta’s platforms since Aug. 15, 2014.

US District Judge James Donato in San Francisco certified those advertisers as a class in 2022. Meta appealed the order to the 9th Circuit and was rebuffed in 2024. The US Supreme Court declined to hear the case in 2025.

With the case back before Donato, Meta in August 2025 “sailed in” with a motion to compel arbitration, the judge wrote in a testy, 8-page order.

The plaintiffs don’t dispute Meta’s arbitration agreements are valid and binding, Donato noted. “This record would seem to present a slam dunk in favor of arbitration, but that is decidedly not the situation,” he wrote in denying the bid.

Instead, he found Meta’s conduct in court --- taking “full advantage of the procedures available” while staying silent about arbitration --- amounted to a waiver of its right to compel arbitration.

On appeal, Meta argues that it could not have moved earlier to arbitrate the unnamed class members' claims because they were not actually parties to the lawsuit until class notice was distributed and the opt-out period closed. Meta says it invoked arbitration 13 days after that happened.

The 9th Circuit panel appeared unconvinced it was quite so simple.

“It’s a pretty clever argument, I’ll give you credit,” said Senior Judge Richard Paez, even as he pressed Deger-Sen why Meta during the fight over class certification didn't argue that most of the proposed members should be excluded because they had arbitration agreements.

Meta says it expressly reserved its right to arbitrate against unnamed class members.

Judge Daniel Collins likewise questioned whether Meta had adequately flagged arbitration. “It’s kind of an important point to tell the district court that you can’t include 80% of the people in the class because they have class action waivers,” he said. “You never said that.”

Nelson also appeared concerned that the class notice did not mention the possibility that Meta would seek to compel arbitration. "It is odd that this didn't get teed up to the class members at all," he said.

Matt Wessler of Gupta Wessler, who represents the plaintiffs' class, told me that if Meta intended to arbitrate, the company should have conveyed it “early and often,” but it failed to do so.

However the court rules, the case is likely to become a guidepost for future defendants weighing when to invoke arbitration agreements. Based on its questions for Meta, the 9th Circuit may decide seven years is too long to scratch that particular itch.

data.title: 'Black Friday' brings consumer spending into focus for AI-rocked market
data.description:
Key points:
  • Anthropic IPO, solid Nvidia earnings fail to lift market
  • Holiday retail sales seen up 4.2%, per Oxford Economics
  • Consumer spending in focus in light of higher prices, energy costs

By Lewis Krauskopf

Investors will turn attention next week to the strength of consumer spending, as they hope evidence of a broadly solid economic backdrop can provide stability for a US stock market that has been shaken by unease about the AI trade.

Next week, "Black Friday" heralds the onrush of the holiday shopping season as retailers offer a wave of discounts. Investors will watch for signs of how consumers are coping with inflation, including rising energy and borrowing costs. Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of the US economy.

"If you continue to see a strong consumer, it should help to lift the economy," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer with Plante Moran Financial Advisors. "That directly contributes back to stronger corporate revenue and earnings growth, and provides a catalyst for investors that extends beyond the AI trade and to other parts of the economy."

Investors are still digesting a steep pullback in heavyweight technology and AI stocks.

This week, the blockbuster market debut from Claude creator Anthropic and a solid quarterly report from beleaguered AI chipmaker Nvidia failed to steady the stock market. Spurred by concerns about heavy financing needs and political pushback, doubts have emerged about the massive spending on data centers and other AI infrastructure that has underpinned the 4-year-old bull market.

"Markets and investors are looking at the tech sector with a lot more questions," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest Wealth Management.

The Anthropic IPO offered investors their first chance to invest in a publicly traded AI lab, and the stock's performance was expected to drive broad sentiment in coming days. Anthropic's shares opened sharply higher on their first day of trading, then pared gains and closed up 17% on Thursday, while major stock indexes sank.

Dragged lower by tech stocks, the S&P 500 <.SPX> was last down 8% from its October 6 all-time high. The technology sector has slumped nearly 19% in that time.

A recent series of technology snafus that disrupted areas from banking to travel to email also left investors edgy heading into a US trading week that will be shortened due to the Thanksgiving holiday.

SOLID OCTOBER RETAIL SALES SETTING HOLIDAY TONE?

Weakness in stocks could threaten consumers' holiday gift-buying, if they feel less wealthy and less likely to spend.

Oxford Economics estimates that holiday retail sales will rise 4.2%, or an increase of 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That covers retail spending in November and December, excluding autos, gasoline, and bars and restaurants.

The National Retail Federation projects 182.7 million consumers plan to shop this year during the five-day Thanksgiving period that runs to "Cyber Monday", citing results from a recent survey. Black Friday is expected to be the most popular day to shop during that period. That overall number would be down slightly from 186.9 million last year, but continues the trend of elevated shopping during the holiday weekend in recent years, the NRF said.

Government data this week showed US retail sales for October increased moderately, while the core measure of such sales rose faster than expected. Retailers including Walmart and Target had upbeat comments or outlooks for the holiday season in their quarterly reports this week.

"The consumer is pretty healthy, and we'd like to see that continue through the end of the year," Nolte said.

COULD GASOLINE PRICES SAP SHOPPING?

Despite solid retail sales data, Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said he was worried "that the consumer is being impacted by higher gas prices, higher energy prices, higher food prices."

The average national price for a gallon of gasoline stood on Thursday at $3.72, according to motorists' group AAA. That is down from nearly $4.30 a month ago, but well above the $3.09 level a year ago.

As the holiday shopping season heats up, Goldman said he was watching the extent of shopping done in stores compared to online, and how much consumers are buying necessities versus discretionary items.

"If the economy exceeds expectations, earnings increase, and earnings drive stock prices," Goldman said.

Investors in the coming week also will monitor reports on inflation and consumer confidence along with an updated read on third-quarter US GDP. Quarterly results are due from Dell Technologies and semiconductor company Analog Devices , which could sway the AI and tech trade.

With just over a month left in 2026, the S&P 500 was on track for a year-to-date gain of nearly 5%. The index had fallen for six straight sessions as of Thursday, and this week dropped below its 200-day moving average — a closely watched trendline — for the first time since April.

"There is a lot to like about the fundamentals" of the market, said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide. "But picking bottoms is difficult when the market is so emotional."

data.title: Why Jeffrey Epstein loved Russia: women, oligarchs and a shot at redemption
data.description:
By David Gauthier-Villars and Mike Spector

Jeffrey Epstein wanted to satisfy a whim. An interior designer had urged the American financier to paint part of his Manhattan townhouse the same color as the famous mauve room inside St. Petersburg’s renowned Alexander Palace. Epstein wanted to see the room for himself.

So, in November 2002, he flew to Russia on his private jet along with British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell and French fashion model scout Jean-Luc Brunel, according to two people familiar with the trip, flight records released by the US Department of Justice and a French prosecutors’ report.

During a layover in Moscow, Epstein, Maxwell and Brunel hopped into bulletproof cars with armed bodyguards to go party at a restaurant with Maxwell’s friend Umar Dzhabrailov, a wealthy Chechen businessman. Afterward, the people said, Epstein told the chauffeur to drive along Tverskaya Street so he could see the prostitutes who lined part of the avenue at night.

Flight records have previously established that Epstein traveled to Russia in 2002, on one of only two known visits he made to the country. But the two people familiar with the trip provided the first account of why he went there and how the journey signaled a deepening engagement with Russia. What began as an obsession with young Russian women and girls evolved into a broader effort to cultivate oligarchs and senior Kremlin officials, and secure a meeting with President Vladimir Putin himself, Reuters found.

Since his death, Epstein has remained a focus of congressional inquiries, court battles and intense public interest. A year after the US Congress forced the Trump administration to release documents from the government's investigations of him, questions persist about his personal relationships with President Donald Trump and other powerful figures. Epstein’s victims and the lawyers representing them continue to seek accountability for his abuse and trafficking of women and girls, even as some face public attacks for speaking out, as Reuters previously reported. Calls for the Justice Department to release more files continue, while investigations connected to Epstein's activities continue in several countries, including Britain and Norway.

Yet significant questions remain unanswered about Epstein's life and trafficking operation – especially his connections to Russia. A lack of hard facts has triggered conjecture and conspiracy theories, including speculation that Epstein had ties to Soviet or Russian intelligence, perhaps through the late Robert Maxwell, Ghislaine Maxwell's father, a British media mogul and suspected triple agent linked to British, Russian and Israeli intelligence.

“Much about Epstein remains unknown,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat, said in a speech in March. “And over and over, it touches Russia.”

Reuters found no evidence that Epstein worked for Russian intelligence, acted on behalf of the Russian government or succeeded in meeting with Putin. Reporters interviewed more than two dozen people familiar with Epstein's ties to Russia, including nine who knew him personally, and reviewed hundreds of pages of US Justice Department records, flight logs, court filings and emails. Putin's office didn’t respond to requests for comment on Epstein.

Epstein’s early interest was largely predatory: recruiting women and underage girls to the US through modeling networks and promises of opportunity. Reuters identified at least 17 women from the former Soviet Union who were drawn into Epstein’s sex-trafficking network, including three of the hundreds who have sought justice for his abuse and exploitation.

But after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to prostitution charges, including soliciting an underage girl, and spending 13 months in jail, Epstein increasingly saw Russia as a pathway back into elite society, Reuters found. He went on to cultivate Russian connections as he sought to rebuild his standing while continuing to recruit women for sex.

Justice Department records show Epstein held Russian visas for much of the period between 2002 and 2019, when he was arrested on federal sex-trafficking charges involving minors and later died in a Manhattan jail at the age of 66. The first of his two known trips to Russia came in 1998, when he visited Sarov, a military-industrial city whose activities were so secret that for decades it didn’t appear on public maps.

The 2002 St. Petersburg visit was his second. On that trip, the group went to Catherine Palace, a former imperial residence that Putin had used to host his US counterpart, George W. Bush, for a bilateral meeting two days earlier. Reuters could not determine if Epstein ultimately went to what’s known as the “Mauve Room” or “Lilac Room” inside the nearby Alexander Palace. His high-profile interior designer, Alberto Pinto, had recommended visiting it.

Documenting Epstein’s relationship with Russia is complicated by a simple fact: many of the central characters are dead.

Epstein’s death in August 2019 was ruled a suicide, as was Brunel's death inside a Paris jail cell in 2022. In March this year, weeks after Dzhabrailov’s name surfaced in the Epstein files, the Russian-Chechen businessman was found with a fatal gunshot wound to his head in his luxury Moscow apartment. Russian state media quoted police sources describing the death as a suspected suicide. Relatives of Epstein and Dzhabrailov have disputed the suicide assessments but no conclusive evidence of foul play has surfaced.

Maxwell is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence in Texas for helping Epstein sexually abuse teenage girls after pleading not guilty and being convicted at trial. In an interview with Justice Department officials last year, she said she could “categorically” attest that Epstein and her father, Robert Maxwell, never met. Her brother, Ian Maxwell, separately told Reuters that, to the best of his knowledge and belief, the two men never crossed paths.

Ghislaine Maxwell’s lawyer declined to comment for this article. In August, a US judge rejected her bid to throw out her conviction and sentence, finding her claims that her rights were violated meritless. She has since filed a motion requesting the court to reconsider.

Despite rarely visiting Russia, Epstein increasingly sought to draw Russian figures into the elite social and professional networks he had spent years cultivating in finance, science, fashion and the arts. From New York, Palm Beach and his private island in the US Virgin Islands, he built relationships that stretched deep into the Russian-speaking world. But the ultimate prize – a meeting with Putin – appeared to elude him.

RUSSIAN WOMEN AND GIRLS

Epstein's embrace of Russia began with its young models.

When the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, and with the Soviet Union starting to open up, Western scouts descended on a vast territory stretching from Prague to Vladivostok in search of new modeling talent.

Among them was French fashion scout Brunel, who worked for Paris-based modeling agency Karin Models. He crisscrossed Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union to recruit girls and young women and bring them to Paris, where US agencies selected talent for the North American market, said Joey Hunter, an American modeling agent who knew Epstein and Brunel.

In September 1991, Brunel hosted a party at his Paris apartment on the upscale Avenue Hoche, said Thysia Huisman, a former model and party guest. She had come from the Netherlands hoping Brunel would help launch her modeling career. Other guests included businessmen, notably from Saudi Arabia, and models from Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Russia, Huisman told Reuters.

One Russian girl, who appeared to be in her early teens, spent much of the evening on Epstein's lap, Huisman said. At the time, Huisman knew him only as "Jeffrey," the name Brunel used. She later recognized him from media coverage as Epstein. The girl told Huisman that Brunel had paid for her ticket to Paris and promised to make her a supermodel.

What struck Huisman most was the girl's age. "It was creepy," she recalled. "The girl said modeling work was not good, but 'Jeffrey takes care of me.' Also creepy was that I was 18, and the girl was clearly a lot younger than me."

Reuters could not independently confirm the party or the identity and age of the Russian girl.

In a 2019 criminal complaint, Huisman accused Brunel of drugging and raping her about a week after the party. Under questioning by French investigators before his death, Brunel denied wrongdoing. He said he first met Epstein on a flight between New York and the French Riviera but didn't say when that happened, noting that he was "not very good with dates," according to the French prosecutors' report. Brunel died while still under investigation and before prosecutors had decided whether to bring him to trial.

Reuters couldn’t independently establish when the two men first met. French prosecutors' records show Brunel described Epstein as a friend and said he traveled in the financier's jet and visited Little St. James, his private island in the US Virgin Islands.

In December 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed. By then, Epstein had amassed millions of dollars from advising Les Wexner, the billionaire retail executive behind the Victoria's Secret lingerie brand. By the mid-1990s, Epstein’s Manhattan townhouse was a hub for celebrities, billionaires and prominent political figures.

A spokesperson for Wexner declined to comment. Wexner has repeatedly denied any knowledge of Epstein's abuse of women and girls, telling the US House Oversight Committee in February 2026 that he was “duped by a world-class con man.”

Epstein was often seen with Russian models and young women. Two managers who worked in the fashion industry and knew the financier recalled the name of one of them: Anna Malova.

In 1993, when she was 22, Malova was a runner-up in the Miss Russia contest in Moscow. She emerged on the US modeling scene in 1996 after competing in the American Dream Calendar pageant in the Bahamas, according to a photograph and two models who also took part. The pageant was a partnership between Trump – who was then a major player in the beauty-contest industry – and businessman George Houraney. Epstein was a regular member of the judging panel and often sat beside Trump, Houraney told Reuters.

Two years later, in 1998, Brunel brought Malova to Karin’s New York office where Hunter, the modeling agent, said Malova signed a contract. Flight records from February 1999 show Malova flew in the financier’s jet from the Caribbean to Palm Beach alongside guests including Maxwell and Britain’s Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor – then known as Prince Andrew.

Malova and a lawyer for Mountbatten-Windsor did not respond to requests for comment. The former prince was stripped of his royal status in 2025 over his ties to the financier. He has denied participating in sex crimes. Karin's current manager in Paris, Ruth Malka, did not respond to requests for comment, but has said the agency cut ties with Brunel in the early 2000s.

Malova's path into Epstein's orbit reflected a pattern that would recur throughout his dealings with Russia: young women were introduced through modeling agencies and beauty pageant networks, then drawn into a circle of wealthy and influential men that overlapped with Little St. James, where US federal prosecutors said Epstein trafficked and abused women and girls.

VISIT TO SAROV

Epstein’s first known trip to Russia, in April 1998, took him to Sarov, the secretive “closed city” where the Soviet Union developed much of its nuclear weapons program. He joined a visit led by Nathan Myhrvold, then a senior executive at US software giant Microsoft, who was touring several cities in search of low-cost software development opportunities, according to an account published that year in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, an academic journal.

Myhrvold, who did not respond to messages seeking comment, has denied being involved in Epstein's criminal activities or ever knowing about them.

The trip has drawn speculation because of Sarov's role in the Soviet nuclear program. Yet little has previously been reported about what Epstein actually did during his brief stay there.

Esther Dyson, an investor and Russian-speaking tech journalist who accompanied Myhrvold as his guide, recalled touring the former home of Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov with Epstein and hearing the financier ask a Russian scientist when he had last been paid. Dyson told Reuters it was never clear to her why Epstein joined the visit, though it appeared he only came to meet Myhrvold and tour the city.

It was one of only two known trips Epstein made to Russia. But many of his ties to the country were cultivated elsewhere, often in glamorous settings frequented by the global elite.

In May 2001, Epstein and Maxwell attended a party on a yacht in St. Tropez, a magnet for celebrities on the French Riviera, to celebrate the birthday of British supermodel Naomi Campbell. At the party, Epstein and Maxwell met Dzhabrailov, the wealthy Russian-Chechen who would host Epstein and Maxwell over dinner in Moscow a year later, according to a person who attended the yacht party.

Dzhabrailov shared Epstein's interest in models and beauty pageants, regularly sponsoring contests and surrounding himself with women, according to people who knew him. Shortly before his death in March, Dzhabrailov described Maxwell in a social-media video as his "soulmate."

Also present at the St. Tropez party was Virginia Giuffre, then 17 years old, according to a photograph taken at the party. Giuffre’s lawyers later said Maxwell had recruited her the previous year, in 2000, while the teen worked as a spa attendant at Trump’s private Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach. Trump and Epstein, who socialized for years, were photographed there with Maxwell that same year.

Maxwell gave a different account. In a 2011 statement later made public in Giuffre’s defamation case against her, Maxwell said Giuffre had told her she was 18. The lawsuit was settled confidentially in 2017, shortly before trial.

Giuffre later accused Epstein of trafficking her to powerful men, including Mountbatten-Windsor. She died by suicide last year. In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Reuters that Trump has been “totally exonerated” on matters involving Epstein. She pointed to a previous White House statement that Trump eventually barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago because he considered him “a creep.”

A lawyer for Campbell said she had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal conduct until his arrest in 2019.

THE RUSSIAN PIPELINE

Epstein’s pipeline of Russian women expanded in 2003, when Brunel opened a Miami modeling agency called Karin Models of America. He renamed it MC2 Models Management two years later. During questioning by French investigators, Brunel said Epstein guaranteed a $300,000 loan to the agency, which was later repaid. Reuters couldn’t independently verify the source or repayment of the loan.

MC2 recruited heavily in Russia and often provided documents for Russian models to travel to the US, while Epstein made apartments available for their housing, two people with direct knowledge of the matter said.

Among the Russian women recruited by MC2 was Svetlana Pozhidaeva. The aspiring model said she met Epstein in Paris in 2008, when she was about 23, and moved to the US the following year after he promised to help her secure a modeling contract with Victoria's Secret, the lingerie company.

She signed with MC2 and the following year became one of Epstein’s personal assistants. In an interview with Reuters, Pozhidaeva said Epstein sometimes gave her Russia-related assignments, including searching for an apartment for him in Moscow – an idea he toyed with, files show, but never carried through. Her main role, however, was massaging Epstein, who routinely sexually abused her, she said.

Within months of being hired, Pozhidaeva said Epstein had entrapped her. Her visa was sponsored by MC2 and her apartment was provided by Epstein. She had no bank account. And her expenses, including healthcare, were covered by Epstein but recorded against her as debt.

Pozhidaeva said she developed an eating disorder because Epstein pressured her about her weight. She slowly became “a shell of myself," she told Reuters. She also feared the financier had political connections, including in Russia, that might allow him to hurt her or her family if she fled, she said.

At one point, Epstein promised to help Pozhidaeva secure a diplomatic job in New York, but the position never materialized. Instead, she said, he encouraged her to take photographs of herself at the United Nations in Geneva and post them online to create the impression of having such a role. She followed his instructions, she said.

Jeff Fuller, the top manager at MC2 at the time, didn’t respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. Florida corporate records show the Miami agency was dissolved in 2019. A similarly named agency in Israel, MC2 Model Management, said it had no formal business ties to the Miami company.

Epstein's network in the former Soviet Union also became a source of introductions to other women. Reuters found that at least nine women from the region, most of them Russians, recommended friends or acquaintances to the financier over the final decade of his life. In a 2013 email, one woman offered to introduce Epstein to three girls she described as attractive and intelligent, while cautioning him not to involve her if he intended to "play" with them.

The woman’s lawyer declined to comment and requested that Reuters not name the woman because she has been formally identified as an Epstein victim in US federal proceedings. Reuters could not independently confirm that claim.

‘TELL PUTIN HE’D BENEFIT’

By late 2009, while serving a year of home detention at his Palm Beach residence, Epstein’s efforts to build relationships with Russian elites intensified. When he encountered wealthy Russians, a person who witnessed such meetings said, he often presented himself as a financial whiz who could help them.

Those he corresponded with included Vladislav Doronin, the Russian real-estate tycoon who was then in a relationship with British supermodel Campbell.

In the spring of 2010, according to emails released by the Justice Department, Doronin's office invited Epstein to a Moscow charity event hosted by Campbell. Epstein did not attend, said a person familiar with the event’s organization.

His home detention ended that July, and later that year he hosted Doronin for dinner at his New York townhouse. Emails show Doronin thanking Epstein for the dinner and the financier giving the Russian tycoon his views on a multimillion-dollar real-estate project in Moscow. Through a spokesperson, Doronin declined to comment.

Epstein also pursued ties to metals billionaire Oleg Deripaska. In 2010, one of Epstein’s assistants sought a meeting through a contact provided by former British cabinet minister Peter Mandelson, according to emails released by the Justice Department. Reuters could not determine whether Epstein and Deripaska met. Two people who knew Epstein said he later exaggerated the extent of his connection with Deripaska. Mandelson’s lawyer and Deripaska’s office didn’t respond to messages seeking comment.

In September 2011, Epstein was planning a trip to Russia that included meetings with a modeling scout and a scientific academy, according to emails released by the Justice Department. In one email chain, an Epstein staff member noted that Epstein's Russian bodyguard, Igor Zinoviev, had said the financier also had an appointment with Putin.

The trip was ultimately canceled, according to the emails and a person who had helped organize it. Three people who knew Epstein said they did not believe any meeting with Putin had actually been scheduled. "It was a charade," one person familiar with the episode said. Zinoviev did not respond to requests for comment.

While in Paris in 2014, Epstein met a man who would become his principal point of contact with Russian official circles, interviews and records reviewed by Reuters show. Sergey Belyakov was the Russian vice minister of economy and an organizer of the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, Russia’s equivalent of the annual Davos gathering.

Over the following years, Epstein and Belyakov kept in close contact, their emails show. During a dinner at his Manhattan townhouse in April 2015, he introduced Belyakov to Ehud Barak, the former Israeli prime minister. Soon afterward, Epstein asked Barak to encourage Belyakov to promote him to Russian leaders.

"I suggest you send (Belyakov) a note," Epstein wrote, "that states that you think Putin and his advisors would benefit from spending some time with Jeffrey to discuss markets, currency and the financial system in the new world of zero interest rates."

Barak didn’t pass on the message, a person familiar with the matter said. Belyakov did not respond to a request for comment.

Epstein also used intermediaries such as Mandelson to help arrange meetings with Putin, apparently with no success.

Epstein made one of his last efforts to cultivate high-level contacts in Russia through an Emirati businessman, Sultan Ahmed Bin Sulayem, the longtime chairman of multinational logistics company DP World.

Their relationship dated back to at least 2005, the Epstein files show.

“Dear sultan,” reads a message from Epstein’s office to Bin Sulayem in January that year. “Jeffrey is wondering what time you would like your massage today in New York.”

Also in 2005, the Emirati businessman attended a Victoria’s Secret fashion show in New York. A photo of the event showed Bin Sulayem and Epstein sitting next to each other in one of the front rows.

In September 2015, Bin Sulayem traveled to Russia to meet with Putin and discuss opportunities to manage the country’s ports, according to an official Emirati government press release. Subjected to growing Western sanctions after annexing the Crimean peninsula from Ukraine in 2014, Russia was eager to open new maritime trade routes.

As Bin Sulayem pursued talks with Russia, Epstein asked him to help find a job for the brother of his assistant, Svetlana Pozhidaeva. "We are going to interview him," Bin Sulayem replied in a 2017 email, though the position never materialized.

Bin Sulayem resigned from DP World in February after his relationship with Epstein became public. Contacted by Reuters, Bin Sulayem hung up when the subject of this article was explained to him. An aide didn't reply to a message seeking comment. DP World did not respond to a request for comment.

Epstein’s courtship of Russia didn’t lead to any big business deals or real influence in the country. A person who knew both Putin and Epstein expressed confidence the two men never met. But the financier left behind a trail of Russian women still seeking justice for his abuse and exploitation.

Another lasting legacy of Epstein’s connection to Russia could be found in New York, where the financier returned after his 2002 trip to St. Petersburg. Photographs show that the walls of the main staircase in his Manhattan townhouse are a similar color to the Mauve Room in the St. Petersburg palace.

data.title: VanEck to end Gemini ETF custody deals, keeps Coinbase
data.description:
VanEck is cutting ties with Gemini as a custodian across three cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs), ending a relationship that began with its first spot Bitcoin ETF.

VanEck notified Gemini on Monday that it would terminate custody and clearing agreements for its Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and Solana (SOL) ETFs, according to separate filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Thursday.

The agreements will end “on or about” Feb. 16, 2027, while Coinbase Custody, which already serves the funds, will continue providing custody services.

The move raises questions about Gemini’s position in the US spot crypto ETF market, where Coinbase serves as custodian for many of the largest funds. The filings did not disclose the reasons for the terminations.

VanEck to also end Gemini’s Solana staking arrangement

The termination extends beyond cryptocurrency custody. VanEck’s Solana ETF (VSOL) filing also covers a Gemini staking services agreement, raising questions about how the fund will handle staking after the transition.

Staking allows tokenholders to earn rewards by helping secure a proof-of-stake (PoS) blockchain such as Solana. For ETFs that stake their holdings, the service can provide an additional source of returns for the fund.

Cointelegraph contacted VanEck and Gemini for comment on the reason for terminating the agreements and the potential impact on the Solana ETF’s staking operations, but had not received a response by publication.

Winklevoss brothers helped pioneer spot Bitcoin ETFs

Gemini’s founders, Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, were among the earliest proponents of spot Bitcoin ETFs in the United States, filing to launch the Winklevoss Bitcoin Trust in July 2013. US regulators did not approve the first spot Bitcoin ETFs until January 2024, more than a decade after the brothers’ initial filing.

Gemini became the original Bitcoin custodian for VanEck’s spot Bitcoin ETF when the fund launched in January 2024, before VanEck added Coinbase Custody in June that year.

VanEck’s Bitcoin ETF (HODL) is considerably smaller than the largest US spot Bitcoin funds, holding about $880 million in assets under management, compared with $47.6 billion for BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) and $10.6 billion for Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), according to Wallet Pilot data as of Thursday.

Gemini has also provided custody services for crypto ETFs in Canada and Australia. In the US, it continues to serve as a custodian for at least one smaller fund, the 7RCC Spot Bitcoin and Carbon Credit Futures ETF (BTCK), which identified Gemini and BitGo as its Bitcoin custodians in a September 2026 regulatory filing.

data.title: Asia report: Nikkei and KOSPI drop 5% as AI sell-off intensifies
data.description:
Asian markets were following in the footsteps of a sell-off on Wall Street overnight despite a blockbuster IPO from Claude maker Anthropic, as investors pulled money away from stocks in the AI and chip sectors. All three benchmark indices in New York lost over 2% each.

The Nikkei 225 tanked 5.1% to a seven-month low, while the broader Topix benchmark fell 3.9%. The KOSPI also tumbled 5.2%, while Taiwan's TAIEX slumped 6.2%.

Elsewhere, the Hang Seng in Hong Kong fell 1.9% while the Shanghai Composite dropped 1.2% and Singapore's STI slipped 2.0%.

“Asian markets rounded off a week from hell as investors dumped tech stocks across the board,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

“Investors are catching up with the news earlier this week that Japanese data centre operator Datasection slashed its annual revenue forecast by 89% due to the cancellation of a major AI infrastructure order. Investors are naturally asking if this is the first domino falling, with the AI build-out story ripe for a potential slowdown."

SoftBank slumped over 14% in Tokyo, with Nikkei-listed Advantest, Kioxia, Tokyo Electron and Fujikura not too far behind.

In South Korea, tech giants Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Samsung Electro-Mechanics all finished with big losses, along with blue chip auto group Hyundai Motor.

Internet technology group NetEase was a heavy faller in Hong Kong after quarterly earnings disappointed, with Q3 revenues down 2% year-on-year to RMB27.9bn. Sector peer Kuaishou Technology also sank after posting a bigger-than-expected loss for the third quarter.

“The slightest bit of bad news is sending shivers down the spines of tech investors as some fear the good times could be over," Mould said.

"The tech trade has always been about accessing fast growth stories, and it’s been a winning ticket to wealth creation for quite some time. Cracks are now appearing in the narrative, and investors seem to be locking in some of their profits."

In economic news, Japanese inflation accelerated to an 11-month high of 2.3% in October from 2.1% in September, while Taiwanese exports surged 79% over last year to a record $124bn in October.
